about: CEGE0100 is a 15-credit, Term 2 first-year module in UCL's Department of Civil, Environmental and Geomatic Engineering (2026/27 module catalogue). It introduces the principles of engineering geology and their use in site analysis, then the basics of soil mechanics: describing and classifying soils, the role of water and effective stress, steady-state seepage and the Mohr circle, alongside laboratory and field skills. In 2026/27 it is assessed by an exam (60%), two pieces of coursework (30%) and an in-class activity (10%). The catalogue lists Atkinson's An Introduction to the Mechanics of Soils and Foundations, Powrie's Soil Mechanics: Concepts and Applications and Waltham's Foundations of Engineering Geology as reading.
topics: Describing and classifying soils; basic properties
The Mohr circle in soil mechanics

notes.h: Rocks, minerals and the processes that make soils
notes.body:
Engineering geology is about the ground as an engineering material: what it is made of, how it formed and how that history controls its strength, stiffness and permeability. In engineering usage, "soil" is any loose or weakly bonded assemblage of particles that can be broken down by hand or gentle agitation, and "rock" is harder, bonded material. The boundary is practical, not geological: a young mudstone and an old stiff clay can behave much alike.

The rock cycle
- Igneous rocks crystallise from molten magma. Intrusive (plutonic) rocks such as granite cool slowly underground and are coarse grained; extrusive (volcanic) rocks such as basalt cool quickly and are fine grained. Fresh igneous rock is usually strong with low porosity.
- Sedimentary rocks form from deposited and cemented particles (clastic: conglomerate, sandstone, siltstone, mudstone) or from biological and chemical deposits (limestone, chalk). They are layered (bedding) and their strength depends strongly on cementation.
- Metamorphic rocks are existing rocks altered by heat and pressure: mudstone becomes slate (with a strong cleavage), then schist and gneiss; limestone becomes marble; sandstone becomes quartzite.

Key minerals
- Quartz: hard (Mohs 7), chemically resistant, so it survives weathering and forms most sand.
- Feldspars: Mohs about 6; they break down by chemical weathering to clay minerals.
- Calcite: Mohs 3; fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid, which is how limestone and chalk are identified in the field.
- Clay minerals (kaolinite, illite, smectite such as montmorillonite) are sheet silicates of tiny, plate-shaped particles with large surface areas. They give fine soils their plasticity; smectites take up water between layers and swell and shrink the most.

Weathering and soil formation
- Physical weathering breaks rock without changing its minerals: freeze–thaw, stress relief on unloading, thermal cycling.
- Chemical weathering changes the minerals: hydrolysis turns feldspar into clay; carbonic acid in rainwater dissolves limestone and chalk, producing solution features (karst, swallow holes).
- Residual soils form in place; transported soils are moved and sorted by agents: rivers (alluvium, terrace gravels), ice (glacial till, often very variable), wind (loess) and gravity (colluvium, head deposits).

Structures that engineers care about
- Discontinuities: bedding planes, joints, faults, cleavage. A rock mass is usually much weaker and more permeable than an intact specimen because of them.
- Orientation is given by dip (the maximum angle below horizontal) and dip direction (or strike, the horizontal line on the plane).
- Folds and faults offset layers, so a stratum found in one borehole may be missing or repeated in the next.

UK examples worth knowing
- The Chalk (Upper Cretaceous) underlies much of south-east England; it is a soft, fractured limestone with solution features.
- The London Clay Formation (Eocene) is a stiff, fissured, high-plasticity clay; it shrinks and swells with changes in water content, which causes subsidence damage near trees.
- Quaternary deposits (glacial till, river terrace gravels, alluvium, peat) blanket much of the country and are often the material you actually build on.

Exam tips: link each rock or soil type to its origin and then to one engineering consequence (strength, permeability, solubility, shrink–swell). Examiners reward the "so what" more than a list of names.

notes.h: Using geology to understand a site
notes.body:
Most geotechnical failures and cost overruns come from ground conditions that were not anticipated. Site analysis aims to build a ground model: a three-dimensional picture of the strata, groundwater and hazards, with engineering properties attached to each unit.

Stages of investigation (BS 5930:2015+A1:2020, the UK code of practice for ground investigations)
- Desk study: collect existing information before anyone drills a hole.
- Site reconnaissance (walkover): look for springs, soft ground, slope movement, old excavations, signs of mining or made ground, and access constraints.
- Ground investigation: intrusive work (trial pits, boreholes, probing, in situ tests) plus groundwater monitoring and sometimes geophysics.
- Laboratory testing on samples, then interpretation and reporting.

Desk study sources
- British Geological Survey maps of bedrock and superficial (drift) deposits, sheet memoirs and archived borehole records.
- Historical Ordnance Survey maps: infilled ponds, pits and railway cuttings often mean made ground.
- Aerial photographs, mining records (for example from the Coal Authority), flood and groundwater information.

Reading geological maps
- Outcrop patterns depend on dip and topography. Horizontal beds follow the contours; vertical beds run straight across the topography.
- The V-rule: where a bed crosses a valley, its outcrop forms a V. Beds dipping upstream V upstream; beds dipping downstream more steeply than the valley floor V downstream.
- Cross-sections are drawn along a line of section. If the section is not parallel to the dip direction you see an apparent dip α, which is never greater than the true dip δ: tan α = tan δ × cos β, where β is the angle between the section line and the dip direction.
- Worked example: true dip 40°, section at 50° to the dip direction: tan α = 0.839 × 0.643 = 0.539, so α ≈ 28.3°.

Intrusive methods
- Trial pits: cheap, shallow, let you see the soil fabric.
- Cable percussion boreholes: the usual UK method in soils; they allow Standard Penetration Tests and the recovery of tube samples.
- Rotary coring: for rock, giving cores from which recovery and fracture spacing are logged.
- Cone penetration testing: a continuous profile of resistance, very good for layering.
- Standpipes and piezometers: groundwater levels and pore pressures, which may vary seasonally.

Geological hazards to look for
- Shrink–swell clays (London Clay, Gault) and trees.
- Dissolution features in Chalk and limestone (sudden collapses).
- Soft compressible alluvium and peat (large settlements).
- Slope instability in clays, including pre-existing slip surfaces.
- Old mine workings, made ground and contaminated land.
- High groundwater and "running" fine sands in excavations.

Eurocode 7
- Geotechnical design in the UK has used BS EN 1997-1:2004+A1:2013 (general rules) and BS EN 1997-2:2007 (ground investigation and testing). The first-generation version classifies projects into three Geotechnical Categories according to complexity and risk.
- Second-generation Eurocode 7 has been published: BS EN 1997-1:2024 (general rules) and BS EN 1997-2:2024 (ground properties), with a third part on geotechnical structures. BSI states that UK adoptions of the first-generation Eurocodes will be withdrawn on 30 March 2028; until then the first-generation documents should be treated as applicable unless a project specifies otherwise.

Exam tips: for any "plan an investigation" question, go in order (desk study, walkover, intrusive work, testing, reporting) and justify each method by the specific geology and hazard of that site.

notes.h: Describing and classifying soils; phase relationships
notes.body:
Soils are described in a standard way so that anyone reading a log knows what was found. In the UK this follows BS EN ISO 14688-1:2018 (identification and description), BS EN ISO 14688-2:2018 (classification) and BS 5930:2015+A1:2020. A typical description: "Firm brown slightly sandy CLAY" (consistency, colour, secondary constituent, principal soil type in capitals).

Particle sizes (BS EN ISO 14688-1)
- Clay: ≤ 0.002 mm; silt: 0.002–0.063 mm; sand: 0.063–2 mm; gravel: 2–63 mm; cobbles: 63–200 mm; boulders: 200–630 mm.
- Coarse soils (sands and gravels) behave mainly according to grading and density; fine soils (silts and clays) according to plasticity and water content.

Grading
- The particle size distribution (PSD) curve plots percentage finer against particle size on a log scale.
- D10, D30, D60 are the sizes at which 10%, 30% and 60% of the mass is finer.
- Coefficient of uniformity Cu = D60/D10; coefficient of curvature Cc = D30²/(D10 × D60).
- A common rule of thumb (from the Unified Soil Classification System) treats a sand as well graded if Cu ≥ 6 and 1 ≤ Cc ≤ 3. Example: D10 = 0.08 mm, D30 = 0.35 mm, D60 = 1.2 mm gives Cu = 15 and Cc = 0.1225/0.096 = 1.28, so well graded.

Plasticity (Atterberg limits)
- Liquid limit wL: water content at which the soil starts to flow like a liquid (in the UK, by the fall-cone test).
- Plastic limit wP: water content at which a thread can no longer be rolled to about 3 mm without crumbling.
- Plasticity index PI = wL − wP.
- Liquidity index IL = (w − wP)/PI; consistency index Ic = (wL − w)/PI = 1 − IL. A soil near IL = 0 is stiff; near IL = 1 it is very soft.
- Plasticity chart: plot PI against wL. Above the A-line, PI = 0.73(wL − 20), the soil is a clay (C); below it, a silt (M). BS 5930 plasticity terms by wL: low (< 35), intermediate (35–50), high (50–70), very high (70–90), extremely high (> 90).
- Example: wL = 62%, wP = 26% gives PI = 36. The A-line at wL = 62 is 0.73 × 42 = 30.7, so the point lies above it: a clay of high plasticity (CH).
- Activity = PI / (% clay-size fraction) indicates which clay minerals are present; smectite-rich clays have high activity.

Phase relationships
Treat the soil as solids, water and air.
- Voids ratio e = Vv/Vs; porosity n = Vv/V = e/(1 + e).
- Water content w = Mw/Ms (mass of water over mass of dry solids).
- Degree of saturation Sr = Vw/Vv; specific gravity of solids Gs (typically 2.65–2.75).
- Key identity: Sr × e = w × Gs. For a saturated soil, e = w × Gs.
- Bulk unit weight γ = (Gs + Sr e) γw/(1 + e); dry γd = Gs γw/(1 + e); saturated γsat = (Gs + e) γw/(1 + e); buoyant γ' = γsat − γw, with γw = 9.81 kN/m³.

Worked example: a 1000 cm³ sample has mass 1950 g and dry mass 1620 g, Gs = 2.70.
- w = 330/1620 = 20.4%.
- ρd = 1.62 Mg/m³, so e = Gs ρw/ρd − 1 = 2.70/1.62 − 1 = 0.667.
- Sr = wGs/e = 0.204 × 2.70/0.667 = 0.825.
- γ = 1.95 × 9.81 = 19.1 kN/m³; γd = 15.9 kN/m³.

Exam tips: write the definition before you substitute numbers, keep w as a decimal in formulas, and sanity-check (e for most natural soils lies roughly between 0.3 and 1.5; Sr cannot exceed 1).

notes.h: Pore water and the principle of effective stress
notes.body:
The single most important idea in soil mechanics is that the behaviour of a saturated soil (its strength and its volume change) is controlled not by the total stress but by the effective stress. Karl Terzaghi developed the principle in the 1920s and stated it formally in 1936.

The principle
- σ' = σ − u, where σ is total stress, u is pore water pressure and σ' is effective stress.
- Physically, σ' is the part of the stress carried through the soil skeleton at particle contacts. Water cannot carry shear stress, so shear strength depends on σ', not σ.

Calculating vertical stresses
- Total vertical stress at depth z: σv = Σ γi hi (plus any surface surcharge q), using the bulk unit weight above the water table and the saturated unit weight below it.
- Hydrostatic pore pressure: u = γw × hw, where hw is the depth below the water table (or below the piezometric level). Above the water table u is usually taken as zero, unless capillary effects are considered.
- σv' = σv − u. A shortcut below the water table in hydrostatic conditions is to use the buoyant unit weight γ' = γsat − γw.

Worked example: sand 0–2 m (γ = 18 kN/m³, water table at 2 m), sand 2–6 m (γsat = 20 kN/m³), clay 6–10 m (γsat = 19 kN/m³). At 10 m depth:
- σv = 2 × 18 + 4 × 20 + 4 × 19 = 192 kPa.
- u = 8 × 9.81 = 78.5 kPa.
- σv' = 113.5 kPa (check: 36 + 4 × 10.19 + 4 × 9.19 = 113.5 kPa).

Situations to reason through
- Raising the water level in a lake above a lake bed adds the same amount to σ and to u at every point in the bed, so σ' does not change.
- Lowering the water table (for example by pumping) reduces u by more than it reduces σ, so σ' increases and the soil compresses. This is why dewatering can cause settlement of nearby buildings.
- Capillary rise above the water table gives negative pore pressure (suction), so σ' is greater than σ there.
- Artesian conditions: if a confined permeable layer has a piezometric level above ground, u at the base of an overlying clay is higher than hydrostatic and σ' is lower. When excavating into the clay, the base can heave once σ' falls to zero. Example: clay 6 m thick (γsat = 19 kN/m³) over gravel with piezometric level 2 m above ground; at the base of the clay u = 8 × 9.81 = 78.5 kPa. Heave occurs when 19(6 − d) = 78.5, i.e. at an excavation depth d ≈ 1.87 m.

Horizontal stresses
- In the ground, the horizontal effective stress is σh' = K0 σv', where K0 is the coefficient of earth pressure at rest. For normally consolidated soils it is often estimated as K0 ≈ 1 − sin φ'. Note that K applies to effective stresses only; you add u back to get total horizontal stress.

Time effects
- In sands, high permeability means pore pressures adjust almost immediately to a change in load. In clays, low permeability means excess pore pressures take time to dissipate, so σ' changes gradually. Short-term (undrained) and long-term (drained) conditions therefore have to be considered separately.

Exam tips: always draw the profile with depths, the water table and unit weights; tabulate σ, u and σ' at every layer boundary; and state your assumption about the soil above the water table.

notes.h: Darcy's law, permeability and flow nets
notes.body:
Water flows through soil from points of high total head to points of low total head. Steady-state seepage means the flow pattern and pore pressures do not change with time.

Heads
- Total head h = z + u/γw (elevation head plus pressure head; velocity head is negligible in soils). Choose a datum and use it consistently.
- Hydraulic gradient i = Δh/L, the head loss per unit length along a flow path.

Darcy's law (Henry Darcy, 1856)
- v = k i and Q = k i A, where v is the discharge (superficial) velocity, k the coefficient of permeability (hydraulic conductivity, m/s) and A the gross cross-sectional area.
- The average velocity of water in the pores is the seepage velocity vs = v/n.
- Typical k: clean gravel above about 10⁻² m/s; clean sands about 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻² m/s; silts about 10⁻⁹ to 10⁻⁵ m/s; intact clays below about 10⁻⁹ m/s. Fissures and sand partings can make field values much larger than laboratory values.
- Hazen's rough empirical estimate for clean sands: k (m/s) ≈ 0.01 × D10², with D10 in mm.

Laboratory tests
- Constant head (coarse soils): k = QL/(A Δh). Example: specimen 100 mm diameter, 150 mm long, head difference 400 mm, 600 mL collected in 120 s. Q = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ m³/s, A = 7.85 × 10⁻³ m², i = 2.67, so k = 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ m/s.
- Falling head (finer soils): k = (aL/(At)) ln(h1/h2), where a is the standpipe area and h1, h2 the heads at the start and end of time t.

Layered soils
- Flow parallel to layers: kh = Σ ki Hi / Σ Hi (dominated by the most permeable layer).
- Flow across layers: kv = Σ Hi / Σ (Hi/ki) (dominated by the least permeable layer).
- Example: 2 m with k = 10⁻⁵ m/s over 1 m with k = 10⁻⁸ m/s gives kh ≈ 6.7 × 10⁻⁶ m/s but kv ≈ 3.0 × 10⁻⁸ m/s.

Two-dimensional flow and flow nets
- For homogeneous, isotropic soil, steady flow satisfies Laplace's equation, ∂²h/∂x² + ∂²h/∂z² = 0.
- A flow net is a graphical solution: flow lines and equipotentials cross at right angles to form curvilinear "squares". Impermeable boundaries are flow lines; boundaries at constant head (for example a river bed) are equipotentials.
- Flow per metre length: q = k H Nf/Nd, where H is the total head loss, Nf the number of flow channels and Nd the number of equipotential drops. Example: k = 3 × 10⁻⁵ m/s, H = 6 m, Nf = 4, Nd = 12 gives q = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s per metre (about 5.2 m³ per day per metre).
- The pore pressure anywhere is found from the head at that point: u = γw(h − z).
- For anisotropic soil, scale horizontal distances by √(kz/kx) and use k' = √(kx kz).

Seepage forces and piping
- Flowing water exerts a seepage force i γw per unit volume in the direction of flow. Upward flow reduces effective stress: σv' = z(γ' − i γw).
- The critical hydraulic gradient, when σv' becomes zero, is ic = γ'/γw = (Gs − 1)/(1 + e), usually close to 1. Sand at this state has no strength ("quick" condition), which can lead to heave or piping at the downstream side of cofferdams and dams.
- A factor of safety against heave is often expressed as ic divided by the exit gradient.

Exam tips: count Nf and Nd carefully (channels between flow lines, drops between equipotentials), give q per metre run with units, and always check the exit gradient against ic.

notes.h: Stress at a point, Mohr circles and the Mohr–Coulomb criterion
notes.body:
The Mohr circle is a graphical way of finding the normal and shear stress on any plane through a point. In soil mechanics, compressive stresses are taken as positive.

Principal stresses
- At any point there are three mutually perpendicular planes with no shear stress: the principal planes. The normal stresses on them are the major, intermediate and minor principal stresses σ1 ≥ σ2 ≥ σ3. In plane problems we work with σ1 and σ3.
- Under level ground, vertical and horizontal planes are usually principal planes, so σv and σh are principal stresses.

Stresses on an inclined plane
For a plane at angle θ to the major principal plane (the plane on which σ1 acts):
- σθ = (σ1 + σ3)/2 + (σ1 − σ3)/2 × cos 2θ
- τθ = (σ1 − σ3)/2 × sin 2θ
- Example: σ1 = 300 kPa, σ3 = 100 kPa, θ = 30°: σθ = 200 + 100 × 0.5 = 250 kPa; τθ = 100 × 0.866 = 86.6 kPa.

Drawing the circle
- Plot σ horizontally and τ vertically. Centre s = (σ1 + σ3)/2; radius t = (σ1 − σ3)/2.
- A plane at θ in the physical element corresponds to a point at 2θ round the circle from the σ1 point.
- The maximum shear stress equals t and acts on planes at 45° to the principal planes.
- The pole (origin of planes) is a point on the circle such that a line from the pole to any stress point is parallel to the plane on which that stress acts. It lets you read plane orientations directly from the diagram.

Total and effective stress circles
- Since u acts equally in all directions and water carries no shear, the effective stress circle has the same radius as the total stress circle but is shifted left by u: s' = s − u, t' = t.

Mohr–Coulomb failure
- Shear strength on a plane: τf = c' + σ' tan φ', where c' is the effective cohesion intercept and φ' the effective angle of shearing resistance.
- Failure occurs when the effective stress circle touches this line.
- For c' = 0: sin φ' = t'/s' = (σ1' − σ3')/(σ1' + σ3'), and σ1'/σ3' = (1 + sin φ')/(1 − sin φ') = tan²(45° + φ'/2).
- The failure plane is inclined at 45° + φ'/2 to the major principal plane.
- Example: c' = 0, φ' = 35°, σ3' = 80 kPa gives σ1' = 80 × tan²(62.5°) = 80 × 3.69 ≈ 295 kPa at failure.
- With c' > 0: sin φ' = (σ1' − σ3')/(σ1' + σ3' + 2c' cot φ').

Mobilised strength
- If a circle lies below the failure line, the angle of the tangent from the origin gives the mobilised angle φmob, with sin φmob = t'/s' (for c' = 0). Comparing φmob with φ' shows how close the soil is to failure.
- Example: σv' = 150 kPa, σh' = 75 kPa: s' = 112.5, t' = 37.5, sin φmob = 0.333, φmob = 19.5°.

Linking to tests
- Shear box: you measure σn' and τf on a known horizontal plane, so each test gives one point on the failure line. Plotting several tests and fitting a line gives c' and φ'.
- Triaxial test: you control σ3 and measure σ1 at failure, so each test gives a whole circle; the envelope is drawn tangent to the circles.

Exam tips: state your angle convention, draw the circle to scale on squared paper if asked, and remember that only effective stresses go on the Mohr–Coulomb diagram.

CEGE0100 includes practical laboratory and field work, and its learning outcomes include presenting information in written and graphical form. Knowing what each test measures, how it works and how to present the data is useful both for the coursework and for exam questions on interpretation.

Laboratory classification tests
- Water content: weigh, dry in an oven at 105–110 °C to constant mass, reweigh; w = mass of water / mass of dry solids.
- Particle size distribution (BS EN ISO 17892-4:2016): sieving for sand and gravel (wet sieving first if fines are present, to wash them through the 63 µm sieve), and sedimentation (hydrometer or pipette) for silt and clay. Sedimentation relies on Stokes' law: small spheres settle at a velocity proportional to the square of their diameter.
- Liquid and plastic limits (BS EN ISO 17892-12:2018+A2:2022): in UK practice the liquid limit is the water content at which an 80 g, 30° cone penetrates 20 mm into the soil paste in 5 s (the standard also allows a 60 g, 60° cone with 10 mm penetration). The plastic limit is the water content at which a rolled thread crumbles at about 3 mm diameter.
- Particle density (Gs) by pycnometer.

Laboratory tests of mechanical and hydraulic behaviour
- Permeability (BS EN ISO 17892-11:2019): constant head for coarse soils, falling head for finer soils.
- Direct shear (shear box, BS EN ISO 17892-10:2018): apply a normal load, shear along a fixed horizontal plane and record shear force against displacement; repeat at different normal stresses and plot peak τ against σn' to obtain c' and φ'.

Field work
- Logging trial pits and boreholes: depth, description to BS EN ISO 14688-1 and BS 5930, sample positions, groundwater strikes and later water levels.
- Standard Penetration Test (BS EN ISO 22476-3:2005+A1:2011): a 63.5 kg hammer falling 760 mm drives a split-spoon sampler. After a 150 mm seating drive, the number of blows for the next 300 mm is the N value. Commonly used density descriptors for sands (the traditional Terzaghi and Peck scale): very loose (0–4), loose (4–10), medium dense (10–30), dense (30–50), very dense (> 50). BS EN ISO 14688-2 gives a different scale based on corrected (N1)60 values, so check which scale your course uses.
- Cone penetration test: a cone with a 60° tip and 10 cm² base area is pushed at about 20 mm/s, recording cone resistance qc and sleeve friction fs (and pore pressure in a CPTu). It gives a continuous profile and is very good for spotting thin layers.
- Simple field tests on fine soils (hand shear vane, thumb pressure) give quick indications of consistency.

Presenting data well
- PSD curves: percentage passing against particle size on a log scale, with the clay/silt/sand/gravel boundaries marked.
- Plasticity chart: PI against wL with the A-line drawn.
- Stress–depth plots: σ, u and σ' against depth, with depth increasing downwards.
- Shear box: τ against σn' with the same scale on both axes so that φ' can be read as an angle.
- Report numbers to sensible significant figures, give units, and state the standard followed.

Uncertainty and quality
- Disturbance during sampling changes the fabric and stress state of clays; sand samples are especially hard to take undisturbed.
- Small specimens may miss fissures and thin layers, so laboratory permeability and strength may not represent the mass.

Exam tips: for a "describe a test" question, give the purpose, apparatus, procedure in a few steps, the calculation, and one limitation.

cards.b: Intrusive (e.g. granite) cools slowly underground and is coarse grained; extrusive (e.g. basalt) cools quickly at the surface and is fine grained.
Calcite (in limestone and chalk) fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid; quartz does not react.
Smectite (e.g. montmorillonite): water enters between its layers, so smectite-rich clays have high plasticity, high activity and large shrink–swell movements.
Chemical weathering in which feldspar reacts with water to form clay minerals such as kaolinite; it is why weathered granite becomes a clayey sand.
Dip is the maximum angle a plane makes with the horizontal; dip direction is the compass bearing of that steepest downward line.
Rock material is the intact rock between discontinuities; the rock mass includes joints, bedding and faults, so it is weaker and more permeable.
Unsorted material deposited directly by ice: a mix of clay, sand, gravel and boulders whose properties vary widely over short distances.
Desk study, site walkover, intrusive ground investigation with in situ tests and groundwater monitoring, laboratory testing, then interpretation and reporting.
tan α = tan δ × cos β, where δ is true dip and β the angle between the section line and the dip direction; apparent dip is never more than true dip.
Where beds dip upstream, their outcrop forms a V pointing upstream as it crosses a valley.

cards.f: Why use historical maps in a desk study?
cards.b: They reveal former ponds, pits, quarries, railways and buildings, which often mean made ground, soft infill or contamination.
The standard UK boring method in soils: allows Standard Penetration Tests and tube samples at intervals, and records groundwater strikes.
BS EN 1997-1:2024 (general rules). BSI will withdraw UK adoptions of first-generation Eurocodes, including BS EN 1997-1:2004+A1:2013, on 30 March 2028.
High plasticity means large shrink–swell movements with seasonal moisture change and tree roots, causing foundation movement.
Clay ≤ 0.002 mm; silt 0.002–0.063 mm; sand 0.063–2 mm; gravel 2–63 mm; cobbles 63–200 mm; boulders 200–630 mm.
PI = wL − wP: the range of water content over which the soil is plastic.
IL = (w − wP)/(wL − wP). Near 0 the soil is at its plastic limit (stiff); near 1 it is at its liquid limit (very soft).
PI = 0.73(wL − 20). Points above it are clays (C); below it, silts (M).
Links degree of saturation, voids ratio, water content and specific gravity of solids; for saturated soil (Sr = 1), e = w Gs.
γsat = (Gs + e) γw / (1 + e), with γw = 9.81 kN/m³.
σ' = σ − u: effective stress is total stress minus pore water pressure. It controls the strength and volume change of saturated soil.
u = γw hw, where hw is the depth below the water table (or piezometric level).
γ' = γsat − γw; useful for σ' below the water table under hydrostatic conditions.

cards.f: Effect of raising lake level on σ' in the bed
cards.b: None: σ and u both increase by γw × rise, so σ' is unchanged.

cards.f: Effect of lowering the water table
cards.b: u falls more than σ, so σ' increases and the soil compresses, which is why dewatering can cause settlement.

cards.f: Base heave in an excavation over an artesian layer
cards.b: Occurs when the weight of soil left above the confined layer no longer exceeds its pore pressure, i.e. σ' at the layer top falls to zero.
Coefficient of earth pressure at rest: σh' = K0 σv'. For normally consolidated soil often estimated as 1 − sin φ'. It applies to effective stresses only.
v = k i (Q = k i A): discharge velocity is proportional to hydraulic gradient; k is the coefficient of permeability in m/s.
h = z + u/γw (elevation plus pressure head) relative to a chosen datum; water flows from high to low total head.
k = QL/(A Δh); used for coarse soils.
k = (aL/(At)) ln(h1/h2), where a is the standpipe area; used for finer soils.

cards.f: Flow per metre from a flow net
cards.b: q = k H Nf/Nd: H is total head loss, Nf the number of flow channels, Nd the number of equipotential drops.
ic = γ'/γw = (Gs − 1)/(1 + e), typically about 1; upward flow at this gradient makes σ' zero (quick condition).
kv = ΣHi / Σ(Hi/ki), controlled by the least permeable layer.
vs = v/n: the average speed of water through the pores, faster than the Darcy (discharge) velocity.

cards.f: Centre and radius of a Mohr circle
cards.b: Centre s = (σ1 + σ3)/2; radius t = (σ1 − σ3)/2, the maximum shear stress.

cards.f: Normal stress on a plane at θ to the major principal plane

cards.b: A rotation of θ in the physical element corresponds to 2θ round the Mohr circle.

cards.f: Total vs effective stress Mohr circles
cards.b: Same radius; the effective circle is shifted left by u because water carries no shear.
τf = c' + σ' tan φ'; failure when the effective stress circle touches this line.
At 45° + φ'/2 to the major principal plane.
105–110 °C to constant mass.
Water content at which an 80 g, 30° cone penetrates 20 mm in 5 s (BS EN ISO 17892-12).
Blows of a 63.5 kg hammer falling 760 mm to drive the sampler 300 mm, after a 150 mm seating drive (BS EN ISO 22476-3).
Settling velocity of a small sphere is proportional to the square of its diameter, so measuring density over time gives the silt and clay size distribution.
Cone resistance qc and sleeve friction fs (and pore pressure in a CPTu) continuously with depth as a 60° cone is pushed at about 20 mm/s.
Medium dense on the traditional Terzaghi and Peck scale (10–30). BS EN ISO 14688-2 instead uses a scale based on corrected (N1)60 values.

cards.f: Why wet-sieve a soil with fines?
cards.b: To wash silt and clay through the 63 µm sieve so they do not cling to coarse grains and are not counted as sand.

questions.q: A pale rock sample fizzes vigorously when dilute hydrochloric acid is dropped on it. Which rock is it most likely to be?
questions.why: Limestone is made mainly of calcite, which reacts with dilute acid and releases carbon dioxide, so it fizzes. Quartzite is metamorphosed sandstone made of quartz, which does not react with acid. Granite is an igneous rock of quartz, feldspar and mica, none of which fizz. Slate is metamorphosed mudstone made of fine silicate minerals, so it does not fizz either.

questions.q: Which clay mineral would you expect to cause the largest shrink–swell movements in a clay soil?
questions.why: Montmorillonite, a smectite, lets water enter between its layers, giving very high plasticity and activity and the largest volume changes. Kaolinite has tightly bonded layers and low activity, so it swells least of the clay minerals. Illite is intermediate. Quartz is not a clay mineral at all: it forms non-plastic silt and sand grains that do not swell.

questions.q: Explain how weathering of a granite can produce a soil, and state two engineering consequences of the resulting material.
markScheme: Physical weathering (e.g. stress relief, freeze–thaw) opens joints and breaks the rock into fragments
Chemical weathering: feldspar hydrolyses to clay minerals while quartz survives as sand-sized grains
Product is a residual clayey sand that may retain relict joints from the parent rock

Consequences: strength and stiffness much lower than fresh rock, varying with depth and weathering grade; permeability and drainage altered; relict joints may act as weak planes (any two, well explained)
questions.modelAnswer: Granite is made of quartz, feldspar and mica. Near the surface, unloading and freeze–thaw open its joints so water can get in. Chemical weathering then attacks the feldspar, which hydrolyses to clay minerals such as kaolinite, while the resistant quartz survives as sand-sized grains. The result, if it stays in place, is a residual clayey sand that may still show the old joint pattern. For engineering, the weathered material is far weaker and more compressible than fresh granite, and its properties change with depth as weathering decreases, so foundations and slopes must be designed for a variable profile. Relict joints can also act as planes of weakness in cuttings.

questions.q: A bed has a true dip of 40°. A cross-section is drawn along a line at 50° to the dip direction. What apparent dip will the bed show on the section?
questions.why: Apparent dip α satisfies tan α = tan δ × cos β = tan 40° × cos 50° = 0.839 × 0.643 = 0.539, so α ≈ 28.3°. 25.7° comes from multiplying the angle itself by the cosine (40° × cos 50°) instead of its tangent. 32.7° comes from using sin 50° instead of cos 50°, which is what you would get if β were measured from the strike rather than the dip direction. 40.0° assumes the section shows the true dip, which only happens when it runs parallel to the dip direction.

questions.q: Under BS 5930, which activity should normally come first when investigating a new site?
options: A desk study of maps and existing records
questions.why: A desk study of geological maps, historical maps and existing borehole records is done first, so that the later investigation can be planned around the expected ground and hazards. Drilling boreholes is intrusive ground investigation, which comes after the desk study and walkover. Laboratory testing needs samples from that investigation. The geotechnical design report is the last stage.

questions.q: A four-storey building is proposed on a site in north London mapped as London Clay, close to large trees, with a stream crossing one corner. Outline a staged site investigation and the main geological hazards it should target.
markScheme: Desk study: BGS maps and borehole records, historical OS maps (infilled ponds, pits, made ground), flood information
Walkover: evidence of soft ground near stream, tree species and positions, cracking in nearby buildings, made ground
Intrusive work: boreholes (e.g. cable percussion) with sampling and in situ testing, trial pits near trees, standpipes or piezometers for groundwater
Hazards: shrink–swell of high-plasticity clay with tree roots; soft alluvium near the stream; made ground or infilled features
Laboratory testing (classification, water content profiles, strength) and reporting with a ground model
questions.modelAnswer: Start with a desk study: BGS bedrock and superficial maps and archived boreholes to confirm the London Clay and any alluvium along the stream, and historical Ordnance Survey maps to find infilled ponds, pits or old buildings that could mean made ground. A walkover then checks the stream banks for soft ground, records the species, height and position of the trees, and looks for cracking in neighbouring buildings. The intrusive investigation should include boreholes with sampling and in situ testing to below the depth of foundation influence, trial pits near the trees to look at roots and desiccation, and standpipes or piezometers to monitor groundwater. Laboratory tests should include Atterberg limits and water content profiles to identify desiccation. The main hazards are seasonal shrink–swell of the high-plasticity clay where trees extract water, soft compressible alluvium near the stream, and any made ground. The findings go into a ground model and an interpretative report.

questions.q: A saturated clay has a water content of 32% and Gs = 2.70. What is its voids ratio?
questions.why: For saturated soil Sr = 1, so e = wGs = 0.32 × 2.70 = 0.864. 0.119 comes from dividing w by Gs instead of multiplying. 0.320 treats e as equal to the water content, leaving out Gs. 0.464 is the porosity n = e/(1 + e), not the voids ratio.

questions.q: A sand has Gs = 2.65 and e = 0.60. What is its saturated unit weight? (γw = 9.81 kN/m³)
questions.why: γsat = (Gs + e) γw/(1 + e) = 3.25 × 9.81/1.60 = 19.9 kN/m³. 16.2 kN/m³ is the dry unit weight Gs γw/(1 + e), which leaves out the water in the voids. 31.9 kN/m³ is (Gs + e) γw without dividing by the total volume 1 + e. 10.1 kN/m³ is the buoyant unit weight γsat − γw.

questions.q: A fine soil has wL = 62% and wP = 26%. How would it be classified on the UK plasticity chart?
questions.why: PI = 62 − 26 = 36. The A-line at wL = 62 gives PI = 0.73 × (62 − 20) = 30.7, so the point lies above the line (clay), and wL between 50 and 70 means high plasticity: CH. Clay of low plasticity comes from reading the plasticity term from the plastic limit (wP = 26%, below 35) instead of the liquid limit. Silt of high plasticity comes from wrongly calculating the A-line as 0.73 × 62 = 45.3, which would put the point below the line. Intermediate plasticity comes from checking the PI of 36 against the liquid limit boundaries of 35–50; the plasticity term depends on wL, not PI.

questions.q: A 1000 cm³ undisturbed sample has a mass of 1950 g; after oven drying its mass is 1620 g. Gs = 2.70. Find its water content, voids ratio, degree of saturation and bulk unit weight.
markScheme: ρd = 1.62 Mg/m³ and e = Gs ρw/ρd − 1 = 0.667
Working shown with correct units
questions.modelAnswer: Mass of water = 1950 − 1620 = 330 g, so w = 330/1620 = 0.204, or 20.4%. Dry density ρd = 1620 g / 1000 cm³ = 1.62 Mg/m³. Since ρd = Gs ρw/(1 + e), e = 2.70 × 1.00/1.62 − 1 = 0.667. Degree of saturation Sr = wGs/e = 0.204 × 2.70/0.667 = 0.825, so the sample is about 83% saturated. Bulk density is 1.95 Mg/m³, so γ = 1.95 × 9.81 = 19.1 kN/m³ (and γd = 15.9 kN/m³).

questions.q: Dry sand (γ = 17 kN/m³) extends from ground level to the water table at 2 m. Below it is saturated sand (γsat = 20 kN/m³). What is the vertical effective stress at 5 m depth? (γw = 9.81 kN/m³)
questions.why: σv = 2 × 17 + 3 × 20 = 94 kPa; u = 3 × 9.81 = 29.4 kPa (3 m below the water table), so σv' = 64.6 kPa. 94.0 kPa is the total stress, with the pore pressure left out. 45.0 kPa comes from measuring pore pressure from ground level (u = 5 × 9.81) instead of from the water table. 70.6 kPa comes from using the saturated unit weight of 20 kN/m³ above the water table as well.

questions.q: The water level in a reservoir rises by 3 m. What happens to the vertical effective stress at a point 2 m below the reservoir bed (soil saturated throughout)?
questions.why: The extra 3 m of water adds 3γw to the total stress and 3γw to the pore pressure, so σ' = σ − u is unchanged. Saying it increases by 3γw counts the extra water load on the total stress but forgets that the pore pressure rises by the same amount. Saying it decreases by 3γw counts the pore pressure rise but forgets the extra total stress. An increase of 3γsat wrongly treats the added layer as saturated soil instead of free water, and still ignores the rise in pore pressure.

questions.q: A 6 m thick clay layer (γsat = 19 kN/m³, water table at ground level) overlies gravel in which the piezometric level is 2 m above ground level. (a) Find the vertical effective stress at the base of the clay. (b) An excavation is dug into the clay (kept dry). At what depth would base heave be expected? (γw = 9.81 kN/m³)
markScheme: (a) σv at base = 6 × 19 = 114 kPa
u at base = (6 + 2) × 9.81 = 78.5 kPa, from piezometric level
σv' = 35.5 kPa
(b) Heave when the weight of remaining clay equals the gravel pore pressure: 19(6 − d) = 78.5
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Total stress at the base of the clay: 6 × 19 = 114 kPa. The pore pressure there is set by the gravel's piezometric level, 8 m above the base: u = 8 × 9.81 = 78.5 kPa. So σv' = 114 − 78.5 = 35.5 kPa, much lower than the 55.1 kPa a hydrostatic profile would give. (b) As clay is removed to depth d, the total stress at the base of the clay becomes 19(6 − d) while the artesian pore pressure stays at 78.5 kPa. Heave occurs when σv' = 0: 19(6 − d) = 78.5, so 6 − d = 4.13 m and d ≈ 1.87 m. In practice a factor of safety would be applied, or the gravel would be depressurised by pumping.

questions.q: In a constant head test, a sand specimen 100 mm in diameter and 150 mm long passes 600 mL of water in 120 s under a head difference of 400 mm. What is k?
questions.why: Q = 600 × 10⁻⁶/120 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ m³/s; A = π × 0.05² = 7.85 × 10⁻³ m²; i = 0.40/0.15 = 2.67; k = Q/(Ai) = 2.39 × 10⁻⁴ m/s. 5.97 × 10⁻⁵ m/s comes from using the 0.1 m diameter as the radius, making the area four times too large. 1.70 × 10⁻³ m/s comes from inverting the gradient (L/Δh instead of Δh/L). 2.86 × 10⁻² m/s uses the collected volume as if it were a flow rate, without dividing by the 120 s.

questions.q: A sand has Gs = 2.65 and e = 0.70. What is its critical hydraulic gradient for upward flow?
questions.why: ic = γ'/γw = (Gs − 1)/(1 + e) = 1.65/1.70 = 0.97. 1.56 is Gs/(1 + e), which is γd/γw: it leaves out the buoyancy (the − 1). 1.97 is (Gs + e)/(1 + e), which is γsat/γw instead of γ'/γw. 2.36 divides by e instead of 1 + e.

questions.q: A flow net under a sheet-pile cofferdam has 4 flow channels and 12 equipotential drops. The total head loss is 6 m and k = 3 × 10⁻⁵ m/s. The last square at the exit (inside the cofferdam) is 0.8 m long in the direction of flow. The sand has γsat = 20 kN/m³. Find the seepage per metre run and the factor of safety against heave at the exit.
markScheme: q = k H Nf/Nd = 3 × 10⁻⁵ × 6 × 4/12 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s per m (≈ 5.2 m³/day per m)
Head loss per drop = 6/12 = 0.5 m
Exit gradient i = 0.5/0.8 = 0.625
FS = ic/i ≈ 1.66, with comment on adequacy
questions.modelAnswer: Seepage: q = k H Nf/Nd = 3 × 10⁻⁵ × 6 × 4/12 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s per metre run, about 5.2 m³ per day per metre. Each equipotential drop is 6/12 = 0.5 m of head, so across the final 0.8 m square the exit gradient is 0.5/0.8 = 0.625. The critical gradient is ic = γ'/γw = (20 − 9.81)/9.81 = 1.04. The factor of safety against heave is 1.04/0.625 ≈ 1.66. This is only modest, so a designer might drive the piles deeper to lengthen the flow path, or add a filter blanket inside the cofferdam.

questions.q: At a point, σ1 = 300 kPa and σ3 = 100 kPa. What are the normal and shear stresses on a plane inclined at 30° to the major principal plane?
questions.why: Centre 200 kPa, radius 100 kPa, and the plane is 2θ = 60° round the circle: σ = 200 + 100 cos 60° = 250 kPa and τ = 100 sin 60° = 86.6 kPa. The pair 286.6 and 50 kPa uses θ instead of 2θ. The pair 150 and 86.6 kPa measures the 30° from the minor principal plane (equivalent to θ = 60°). The pair 300 and 173.2 kPa uses the diameter (σ1 − σ3) where the radius should be.

questions.q: A dry sand has c' = 0 and φ' = 30°. In a triaxial test with σ3' = 100 kPa, what is σ1' at failure?
questions.why: σ1'/σ3' = (1 + sin 30°)/(1 − sin 30°) = 1.5/0.5 = 3, so σ1' = 300 kPa. 33.3 kPa inverts the ratio, using (1 − sin φ')/(1 + sin φ'), which would make σ1' smaller than σ3'. 150 kPa uses only the numerator (1 + sin φ'). 173.2 kPa uses tan(45° + φ'/2) = tan 60° without squaring it.

questions.q: Three shear box tests on a sand give peak shear stresses of 41, 70 and 128 kPa at normal effective stresses of 50, 100 and 200 kPa. Determine c' and φ', and find the major principal effective stress at failure in a triaxial test on the same soil with σ3' = 60 kPa.
markScheme: Plot τ against σn' with equal scales; points lie on a straight line
Intercept c' = 41 − 0.58 × 50 = 12 kPa
Use sin φ' = (σ1' − σ3')/(σ1' + σ3' + 2c' cot φ') or Mohr circle tangent to envelope
σ1' ≈ 222 kPa (221.6 kPa if φ' is rounded to 30°)
questions.modelAnswer: Plotting τ against σn' gives a straight line through all three points. Slope = (128 − 41)/(200 − 50) = 0.58, so φ' = tan⁻¹ 0.58 = 30.1°, about 30°. Intercept c' = 41 − 0.58 × 50 = 12 kPa (check: 12 + 0.58 × 100 = 70 kPa). For the triaxial test, failure requires sin φ' = (σ1' − σ3')/(σ1' + σ3' + 2c' cot φ'). With φ' = 30.1°, sin φ' = 0.502 and c' cot φ' = 12/0.58 = 20.7 kPa. So σ1' − 60 = 0.502(σ1' + 60 + 41.4), which gives 0.498 σ1' = 60 + 50.9, so σ1' ≈ 222 kPa. Using φ' = 30° exactly: σ1' = σ3' tan²60° + 2c' tan 60° = 180 + 41.6 = 221.6 kPa. Either way, about 222 kPa.

questions.q: During a Standard Penetration Test, the blow counts for six successive 75 mm increments are 3, 4, 5, 6, 6 and 7. What is the SPT N value?
questions.why: The first two increments (150 mm) are the seating drive and are not counted; N is the number of blows for the next 300 mm: 5 + 6 + 6 + 7 = 24. 31 adds all six increments, including the seating drive. 7 is the seating drive alone (3 + 4). 11 counts only the first 150 mm of the test drive (5 + 6).

questions.q: In the UK fall-cone test using an 80 g, 30° cone, the liquid limit is the water content at which the cone penetrates:
options: until the soil thread crumbles at 3 mm
questions.why: For the 80 g, 30° cone the liquid limit corresponds to 20 mm penetration in 5 s. 10 mm is the criterion for the alternative 60 g, 60° cone, not the 80 g cone. 25 mm confuses the test with the Casagrande cup method, where the groove closes after 25 blows. A thread crumbling at about 3 mm is the plastic limit test, not the liquid limit.

questions.q: A soil has 25% passing the 63 µm sieve. Describe how its particle size distribution would be determined in the laboratory, and calculate Cu and Cc if D10 = 0.08 mm, D30 = 0.35 mm and D60 = 1.2 mm.
markScheme: Oven-dry and weigh; wet sieve through 63 µm to remove fines, dry and dry-sieve the retained coarse fraction through a nest of sieves
Sedimentation (hydrometer or pipette) on the fine fraction, based on Stokes' law
Combine results into a PSD curve of % finer against log particle size
Interpretation: well graded by the usual criteria (Cu ≥ 6, 1 ≤ Cc ≤ 3)
questions.modelAnswer: Because a quarter of the soil is finer than 63 µm, sieving alone is not enough. A dried, weighed sample is wet sieved through the 63 µm sieve to wash out the fines, then the retained material is dried and passed through a nest of sieves, weighing what is retained on each. The fines are analysed by sedimentation (hydrometer or pipette): particles settle at speeds given by Stokes' law, so density measurements over time give the proportion finer than each size. The two sets of results are combined into one curve of percentage finer against particle size on a log scale (BS EN ISO 17892-4). From the given sizes, Cu = D60/D10 = 1.2/0.08 = 15 and Cc = D30²/(D10 × D60) = 0.1225/0.096 = 1.28. With Cu well above 6 and Cc between 1 and 3, the coarse part of the soil is well graded.

questions.q:
A site has the following profile: 0–7 m sand, 7–15 m clay, then impermeable rock. The water table is initially at 3 m depth. Unit weights: sand above the water table 17 kN/m³; sand below the water table 20 kN/m³; clay 18.5 kN/m³ (saturated). Take γw = 9.81 kN/m³.
(a) Calculate σv, u and σv' at 3 m, 7 m, 11 m and 15 m depth and sketch the profiles. [8]
(b) Dewatering lowers the water table permanently to 5 m depth; the sand between 3 m and 5 m drains to a unit weight of 17 kN/m³. Calculate the new long-term σv' at 11 m and the change in effective stress. [6]
(c) Explain why the change in effective stress in the clay would not happen immediately, and what consequence the change has for nearby structures. [6]
markScheme: (a) σv correct at all four depths: 51, 131, 205, 279 kPa
(a) u from the water table: 0, 39.2, 78.5, 117.7 kPa
(a) σv' = 51.0, 91.8, 126.5, 161.3 kPa, with a correctly shaped sketch (linear within layers, change of slope at boundaries)
(b) New u at 11 m = 6 × 9.81 = 58.9 kPa, so σv' = 140.1 kPa; increase ≈ 13.6 kPa
(c) Low permeability of clay delays the drop in pore pressure; σ' rises gradually as water drains
(c) Increase in σ' causes compression of the clay and settlement, possibly differential, of nearby foundations; mention monitoring or limiting drawdown
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Total stress uses 17 kN/m³ above the water table, 20 kN/m³ for saturated sand and 18.5 kN/m³ for clay; pore pressure is hydrostatic from the water table at 3 m.
- 3 m: σv = 3 × 17 = 51 kPa; u = 0; σv' = 51.0 kPa.
- 7 m: σv = 51 + 4 × 20 = 131 kPa; u = 4 × 9.81 = 39.2 kPa; σv' = 91.8 kPa.
- 11 m: σv = 131 + 4 × 18.5 = 205 kPa; u = 8 × 9.81 = 78.5 kPa; σv' = 126.5 kPa.
- 15 m: σv = 205 + 4 × 18.5 = 279 kPa; u = 12 × 9.81 = 117.7 kPa; σv' = 161.3 kPa.
The profiles are straight lines within each layer. σv' increases at 17 kPa/m above the water table, 10.19 kPa/m in the saturated sand and 8.69 kPa/m in the clay; u is zero to 3 m and then increases at 9.81 kPa/m.

(b) After dewatering, at 11 m: σv = 5 × 17 + 2 × 20 + 4 × 18.5 = 85 + 40 + 74 = 199 kPa. The water table is now 6 m above this point, so u = 6 × 9.81 = 58.9 kPa. σv' = 199 − 58.9 = 140.1 kPa. The increase is 140.1 − 126.5 = 13.6 kPa. Total stress has fallen slightly (by 6 kPa, because 2 m of sand lost water), but pore pressure has fallen by 19.6 kPa, so the effective stress rises.

(c) The sand is permeable, so its pore pressures adjust almost at once. The clay has a very low permeability (typically below 10⁻⁹ m/s), so water can only leave it slowly. Immediately after dewatering, pore pressures in the clay remain close to their original values and σ' changes little. As water drains towards the sand over months or years, u falls to the new hydrostatic values and σ' rises towards the long-term value found in (b). Because the clay's volume depends on σ', it compresses as σ' increases, and the ground surface settles. Nearby buildings on shallow foundations may experience settlement, which is often uneven where the drawdown varies across a building. Engineers therefore monitor groundwater levels and settlement, limit the drawdown (for example with cut-off walls or recharge wells), or assess the neighbours' tolerance to movement in advance.

questions.q:
An element of saturated sand beneath level ground has σv' = 150 kPa and σh' = 75 kPa. The sand has c' = 0 and φ' = 32°.
(a) Draw the Mohr circle of effective stress, giving its centre and radius. [3]
(b) Find the normal and shear effective stresses on a plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. [4]
(c) Find the mobilised angle of shearing resistance and comment on how close the element is to failure. [4]
(d) If σv' stays constant and σh' is gradually reduced (for example as a retaining wall moves away from the soil), find σh' at failure and the inclination of the failure planes. [5]
(e) Alternatively, if the total stresses stay constant but the pore pressure rises, by how much must u increase to cause failure? [4]
markScheme: (a) Vertical and horizontal planes are principal; s' = 112.5 kPa, t' = 37.5 kPa
(b) Horizontal plane is the major principal plane; 2θ = 60°: σ' = 112.5 + 37.5 cos 60° = 131.3 kPa
(c) sin φmob = t'/s' = 0.333, φmob = 19.5°; well below φ' = 32°
(d) Failure planes at 45° + φ'/2 = 61° to the horizontal (major principal plane)
(e) Radius constant at 37.5 kPa; failure when s' = t'/sin φ' = 70.8 kPa, so Δu = 112.5 − 70.8 ≈ 41.7 kPa
Clear diagrams and correct use of effective stresses throughout
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Under level ground there is no shear on horizontal or vertical planes, so σv' = 150 kPa is σ1' (acting on the horizontal plane) and σh' = 75 kPa is σ3'. Centre s' = (150 + 75)/2 = 112.5 kPa; radius t' = (150 − 75)/2 = 37.5 kPa. The circle passes through (75, 0) and (150, 0).

(b) The horizontal plane is the major principal plane, so a plane at 30° to the horizontal is at θ = 30°, or 2θ = 60° round the circle.
σ' = 112.5 + 37.5 cos 60° = 112.5 + 18.75 = 131.3 kPa.
τ = 37.5 sin 60° = 32.5 kPa.

(c) The tangent from the origin to the circle makes an angle φmob with sin φmob = t'/s' = 37.5/112.5 = 0.333, so φmob = 19.5°. That is well below φ' = 32°: tan φmob/tan φ' = 0.354/0.625 ≈ 0.57, so only about 57% of the available frictional strength is mobilised (a factor of safety on tan φ' of about 1.8). The element is far from failure.

(d) With σv' fixed as σ1' and σh' falling, the circle grows to the left until it touches the failure line. For c' = 0, σ3'/σ1' = (1 − sin φ')/(1 + sin φ') = (1 − 0.530)/(1 + 0.530) = 0.307. So σh' = 150 × 0.307 = 46.1 kPa at failure. The failure planes are inclined at 45° + φ'/2 = 45° + 16° = 61° to the major principal plane, which is horizontal, so they dip at 61° to the horizontal.

(e) If total stresses are constant, a rise in u shifts the effective stress circle to the left without changing its radius (37.5 kPa). Failure occurs when the circle touches the line τ = σ' tan 32°, i.e. when t'/s' = sin 32°: s' = 37.5/0.530 = 70.8 kPa. The centre must move from 112.5 to 70.8 kPa, so u must rise by about 41.7 kPa (about 4.3 m of extra water head). At that point σ1' = 108.3 kPa and σ3' = 33.3 kPa, whose ratio is again 0.307, confirming failure. This is why rising pore pressures, for example after heavy rain, can trigger failures without any change in load.
